title: Warnings Are Visible But Not Actionable
excerpt: Warnings can be visible without being actionable when their format, timing, hierarchy, or interface architecture does not match operating conditions. In high-consequence contexts, a warning must be perceivable, interpretable, and usable at the moment it appears.
metaDescription: Why visible warnings fail when operators cannot recognise, interpret, or act on them under real use conditions.
summary: This situation describes warning systems that are present in the interface but fail under operating conditions. The documented failure modes are format failure, timing failure, gradient failure, and architecture failure, with examples from medical devices, safety-critical simulation software, e-bike displays, maritime systems, automotive controls, and hospital dispatch interfaces.
definition: Warnings are visible but not actionable when an operator can see that a warning exists but cannot process, interpret, prioritise, or respond to it correctly under the conditions that produced it.
keyFacts: A warning is treated as a communication act, not only as a visual design element.
IEC 62366-1 frames a warning that cannot be acted on under use conditions as a use-related hazard in medical-device usability engineering.
Format failure occurs when a warning requires reading in conditions where only rapid recognition is available.
Timing failure occurs when a warning appears at a point in the workflow where acting on it would create a second hazard or excessive corrective load.
Gradient failure occurs when all warnings carry similar visual weight, making urgent and advisory states initially indistinguishable.
Architecture failure occurs when warnings are added after layout and interaction rules are fixed, leaving no structural place for interruptive states.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, eight surgeons reported during 13 structured design review sessions that device state could be verified through brief glances after warning redesign; this was not post-deployment operational measurement.
In the Gexcon engagement, client-measured configuration errors reduced from 5–8 per simulation to 1–2 per simulation, and corrective load reduced from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.

In the Stromer engagement, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of issues requiring user intervention before redesign and did not appear on the issues list after redesign in the same structured test protocol.

Raymarine prototype testing recorded seven of eight participants recognising and correctly classifying the risk event, with median recognition latency of 3.60 seconds and a range of 2.1 to 8.2 seconds.
bodyMarkdown:
## Warning visibility is not the same as warning actionability

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A warning is not only a design element. A warning is a communication act that must answer whether the operator can perceive, interpret, and act on it correctly in the conditions that produced it.

In high-consequence operational contexts, warning design cannot be evaluated only by asking whether the warning is present or visually prominent. A warning that requires reading is not functional where only a glance is available. A warning that relies on colour as its primary signal is not functional where lighting makes colour distinction unreliable. A warning that appears in the middle of a task sequence can force a choice between responding to the warning and completing the primary task safely.

IEC 62366-1, the international standard for usability engineering of medical devices, treats a warning that cannot be acted on under use conditions as a use-related hazard. In that framing, the presence of a warning is not evidence that risk has been addressed. Evidence is needed that the warning can be perceived, interpreted, and acted on under the identified use scenarios and environments.

## Format failure occurs when warnings require reading but only recognition is available

Format failure occurs when a warning is encoded as text, a code, or a labelled state in an operating context where the operator does not have time or attention available for reading. A text warning that is legible at a desk can fail during a surgical procedure, a vessel manoeuvre, or a high-throughput operational task.

The design response described in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method is pattern-based recognition. Warning states communicate through visual form rather than verbal content: shape, spatial arrangement, contrast, and redundant cues that can be decoded in a glance.

Pattern-based warning recognition is used in contexts such as medical device standards, aviation alerting design, and industrial control systems. The source distinction is not that symbols automatically solve warning design, but that warning format must match the actual conditions of use.

## Timing failure occurs when acting on the warning would create a second hazard

Timing failure occurs when a warning appears at a point in a sequenced workflow where the operator cannot safely respond without abandoning or disrupting the primary task. The interface then creates a double-bind: ignore the warning and continue, or respond to the warning and interrupt the workflow.

The design response in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method is contextual warning placement. The task sequence must be understood well enough to place warning communication at points where the operator can evaluate the warning and respond without creating a second hazard.

This requires domain learning. The workflow must be understood from inside the task, not only from a functional specification.

## Gradient failure occurs when all warnings carry similar visual weight

Gradient failure occurs when warning saturation makes urgent and advisory states initially indistinguishable. In systems that evolve by accumulation, every possible risk condition can become a warning. If all warnings use the same visual weight, operators develop a single first response to all warnings: check, assess, proceed.

In clinical or safety-critical contexts, the time required to distinguish a critical alert from an advisory can be the gap between a managed risk and an unmanaged one. The design response is a warning hierarchy with consequence-differentiated visual grammar. The interface must communicate not only that attention is required, but what class of attention is required.

## Architecture failure occurs when warnings are added after layout and interaction rules are fixed

Architecture failure occurs when warning design is treated as an additive visual step instead of a structural interface decision. If screen architecture, interaction logic, and layout rules are established first, warnings have no native relationship to the surface they inhabit.

Warnings created this way can cover content they should not cover, appear at moments the interaction model cannot accommodate, or interfere with active tasks because the interface did not reserve space or timing for them. The warning is present, but the interface was not built to receive it.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats warning behaviour as an architectural decision. The rules governing warnings, overlays, and interruptive states must be established before component design fixes the surface.

## deSoutter Medical / Zethon showed format failure in surgical device warnings

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement concerned an embedded GUI for a powered ultrasonic bone cutter used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery. The device operates at high rotational speeds and is subject to IEC 62366-1 usability engineering requirements.

Surgeons check device state, readiness conditions, and warnings through brief glances while maintaining sterile position, managing the patient, and coordinating with surgical assistants. Use typically occurs with the non-dominant hand, through gloves, and under variable theatre lighting.

The legacy interface presented warnings as text. Under controlled viewing conditions, the text was legible. Under actual surgical conditions, a warning that required reading created a moment where the surgeon had to shift attention from the patient to the interface long enough to read, parse, and interpret a statement. In the context described, format failure in an operating theatre is a use-related hazard under IEC 62366-1.

Benchmarking of six comparable surgical devices during Sandbox Experiments identified reliance on colour as the primary warning signal across the category. Under ideal theatre lighting, colour-based warnings functioned adequately. Under the range of lighting conditions present in real operating theatres, colour distinction was unreliable.

Creative Navy's redesign applied pattern-based recognition throughout the warning system. Critical states were communicated through spatial arrangement, redundant non-colour cues, and high-contrast differentiation that did not rely on colour alone. Creative Navy-recorded reports from eight surgeons across 13 structured design review sessions indicated that device state could be verified through brief glances without reading, and that warning presentation no longer required attention to be pulled from the surgical field for interpretation. This was not post-deployment operational measurement.

Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

## Gexcon showed timing failure at workflow scale in simulation setup

Gexcon's CFD simulation software is used by engineers performing gas dispersion modelling, explosion risk assessment, and facility safety validation for industrial installations. Before Creative Navy's engagement, the interface did not communicate clearly where in a simulation setup an error had occurred.

Engineers completing a scenario configuration received output that appeared valid, but configuration errors averaging 5–8 per simulation were embedded in it. Error discovery was deferred until output review or until a simulation had to be re-run. Corrective work took 4–6 hours.

This is timing failure at workflow scale. Configuration warnings were not surfaced during the configuration step, before the simulation ran, when correction was straightforward.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed this through an error-prevention interaction architecture. The work specified which values had to remain visible during scenario setup, where warnings were needed before the simulation ran, and how the system should respond to incomplete or contradictory input.

Gexcon client-measured the result across real deployment locations: configuration errors reduced to 1–2 per simulation, and corrective load reduced to approximately 20 minutes.

## Stromer showed warning architecture failure on an e-bike embedded display

Stromer manufactures premium e-bikes whose interface spans an embedded display on the bike, a mobile companion app, and a web account. The embedded display is used while riding, where the rider's eyes leave the road to read or recognise displayed state.

The embedded display carried safety warnings, status alerts, error states, and threshold notifications. EN 15194:2017, the European standard for electrically power-assisted cycles, specifies requirements for warning device behaviour and symbol conventions.

Before Creative Navy's engagement, a previous external agency had completed a year-long design engagement that produced a design system and visual redesign work. The unresolved structural problem was warning architecture. Warnings were layered onto a screen architecture that had already been set.

The consequences were observable in use: warnings covered parts of the screen they should not cover, interfered with active interactions, were difficult to dismiss in context, and frequently appeared without enough contextual information for the rider to understand what they were about.

Creative Navy's redesign addressed the layout and overlay system, the information architecture, and the rules governing how warnings and other interruptive elements relate to screen structure across states and warning types.

Creative Navy designed and ran a structured test methodology. Ten participants rode the bike over three days each on real routes in Munich and surrounding countryside, logging every issue encountered with severity on a four-level scale: interference, annoyance, issue needing user intervention, and critical issue. Before redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of all issues rated as requiring user intervention. After redesign, the same test was run with 10 users, six from the original cohort and four replacements, using the same bikes, routes, and logging protocol. Warnings did not appear on the issues list. Creative Navy ran the same test again two years later; warnings remained absent.

## Streetec showed neutral escalation for normal operations

Streetec's kntrl 2 control system for aftermarket automotive air suspension used a two-level alert escalation. A first attempt at a blocked action produced an inline notification. A second attempt produced a modal.

The design kept colour neutral until a genuine alert state. Raising and lowering pressure were both normal operations, so neither was colour-coded as a warning. This preserved the palette's signalling power for conditions that needed it.

## The MDU showed an alarm that is actionable even when the interface does not actuate control

The MDU is a ship motion monitoring system whose bridge interface Creative Navy designed. The system is deliberately non-actioning: it may alarm and nothing else. Actions based on the GUI data are made elsewhere, such as changing course, changing speed, deploying stabiliser fins, or consulting shore-based advice.

The alarm remains useful because it states a condition precisely enough to support action outside the interface. Alarm state binds to the rolling maximum and minimum, so an alarm means the vessel was outside its threshold at some point within the last twenty minutes. A three-arrow mechanism shows the interval of movement beside the alarm: one arrow for the current position, two arrows for the minimum and maximum of the rolling window, and a shaded band between them.

The MDU alarm stakes are calibrated as comfort, cargo, and crew-safety alarms rather than immediate-danger alarms. No safety outcome, alarm-response figure, regulatory credential, or user-tested result attaches to the MDU engagement.

## Raymarine showed consequence-based alert priority in a prototype test

In the Raymarine engagement for the next generation of Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF line, Creative Navy assigned four event priority levels by consequence rather than arrival order.

Emergency events, including outgoing distress, received distress, and local man overboard, took a persistent incident surface that no ordinary action dismissed. High concern events, including a qualifying proximity risk or urgency event, were prominent and actionable with their source visible, and never silently altered a radio control. Operational events, including an incoming routine call, a degraded data condition, or a blocked action, were noticeable and proportionate, and did not silently change the selected vessel or tuned channel. Background events, including a new target or routine status change, updated quietly and never took keypad focus.

Creative Navy designed the test protocols, moderated all 24 sessions, and analysed the results on a bench mockup supplied by Raymarine. The recognition finding was recorded as counts from eight participants: seven of eight participants recognised the risk event and classified it correctly, with median recognition latency of 3.60 seconds and a range of 2.1 to 8.2 seconds. One occasional operator first classified the proximity warning as a general system notification.

These findings describe behaviour on a prototype against a fixed fixture. They are not safety results and are not claims about the released radio's performance.

## Maritime traffic monitoring showed why one chronological notification surface was rejected

In an engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations, and waterway operators, the audit found traffic conditions, equipment faults, and advisory notices sharing one notification surface.

Ordering by receipt time could be mistaken for operational priority. Acknowledgement, dismissal, and resolution used overlapping wording. Action history could carry visual weight comparable to the current lifecycle state.

Creative Navy's designed response was typed alerts over a unified queue. A single chronological notification queue was rejected because it mixed navigation alerts with technical faults. A filtered single list was rejected because the current filter could hide a class of important event, and a count alone could not explain technical degradation during a traffic task.

The selected model presented navigation alerts by operational priority and lifecycle, with equipment health in its own typed view carrying an impact explanation. Both were cross-linked from a common event history. No safety, certification, or conformity credential attaches to this engagement.

## Oceaneering showed a saturated warning channel in hospital dispatch

For Oceaneering's hospital dispatch panel, the predecessor record described an error with no stated cause. If staff chose the wrong cart type, the vehicle arrived, tried to lift, detected the wrong cart, set it down, and left without explaining why.

The physical indication was not meaningful in context. The vehicle sat beneath the cart flashing its lights, but staff did not notice because the lights were always flashing when the vehicles moved. The warning channel existed, but it had been saturated into normal operation.

This account comes from the predecessor's specification and from interviews with people adjacent to the users. No depot was visited, and no redesign outcome was measured.

## Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses warning actionability through domain learning and performance in reality

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses warning actionability by grounding warning design in the conditions under which warnings are encountered. The shared root of format failure, timing failure, gradient failure, and architecture failure is that the warning was designed for a user with time, attention, and controlled viewing conditions, not for the operator who actually encounters it.

Domain learning is the prerequisite. In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, 13 structured sessions with eight surgeons documented when surgeons checked device state and which moments in the surgical workflow were sensitive to attention being drawn away. In the Gexcon engagement, understanding the simulation workflow made it possible to position warnings before the simulation ran. In the Stromer engagement, analysing the previous agency's work helped diagnose why surface redesign had not resolved the underlying warning architecture.

Performance in reality is the evaluation standard. A warning is not evaluated only on a screen at close range. It is evaluated under the lighting, time pressure, physical constraints, workflow interruptions, and interaction states of actual operation. IEC 62366-1 makes this a regulatory requirement in the medical-device context described here; in the other contexts on this page, it remains the practical condition that determines whether a warning works.

## Evidence boundaries for warning actionability claims

The evidence on this page is case-specific. The deSoutter Medical / Zethon evidence is formative and based on Creative Navy-recorded reports from surgeons during structured design review sessions, not post-deployment operational measurement.

The Gexcon figures are client-measured across real deployment locations. The Stromer warning outcome is Creative Navy-recorded from a structured methodology that Creative Navy designed and ran. The Raymarine recognition finding is a prototype test result on a bench mockup and is reported as counts, not percentages or population claims.

The MDU engagement has no safety outcome, alarm-response figure, regulatory credential, or user-tested result. The maritime traffic monitoring engagement has no safety, certification, or conformity credential attached to the design work. The Oceaneering account has no measured redesign outcome and did not include a depot visit.

## Related documentation

This situation relates to documented cases and adjacent situation pages where warning actionability, system-state recognition, operational timing, and recovery from errors affect real work. Relevant documented cases include Stromer, Raymarine, the MDU, Streetec, and Oceaneering. Related situation pages include system state that is hard to understand, abnormal conditions that break the interface, delayed understanding that creates risk, interfaces that increase cognitive load at the worst moment, and users who cannot recover cleanly from errors.
